source.title: SpanSeq: similarity-based sequence data splitting method for improved development and assessment of deep learning projects
source.authors: Alfred Ferrer Florensa; J. J. Almagro Armenteros; Henrik Nielsen; F. Aarestrup; P. L. C. Clausen

record.file_problem: The supplied text appears to contain the full paper. Figure values are not transcribed, so several outcomes are available only as qualitative descriptions.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares similarity-aware, random, and increased-similarity data partitions and reports their effects on model development and held-out performance. This bears on generalization assessment, but it does not test the specific interventions named in V1–V8.
record.gate_note: The study reports effects of data-splitting strategy, an intervention not represented by the listed versions. Its introductory statements about fitting random labels and dropout or weight decay are background citations, not results from this study.
record.test_reason: The study tests sequence-similarity-aware data partitioning and its effects on validation and evaluation. None of its experiments tests the interventions or comparisons in V1–V8. Random partitions are not random labels, and near-perfect natural-label training fit does not establish V1.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately paraphrases the authors' conclusion: similarity-aware partitions reduce inflated generalization estimates, protect validation-based development from similarity leakage, and can reduce development resources. These are the authors' claims; RNA leakage may remain, resource savings are inferred from earlier validation optima, and improved holdout performance is not established conclusively.
record.recipe_differences: The study changes dataset partitioning by sequence similarity; it does not test the claim versions' model interventions or measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Partition strategy changes training curves, validation behavior, and the relationship between test and holdout-test performance. The authors note that the RNA similarity threshold may be insufficient, allowing some leakage.

fits_no_version.finding: Random and increased-similarity partitions yield higher validation and ordinary test performance than similarity-restricted holdout performance; SpanSeq test and holdout performance are described as nearly equal. RNA results retain possible similarity leakage.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For biological sequence predictors, similarity across development and test partitions can inflate estimates of performance on dissimilar sequences.

fits_no_version.finding: Partition strategy changes validation trajectories and the epochs selected as best, with earlier validation optima under SpanSeq; DL-RNA training curves remain similar across strategies.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Similarity-aware partitioning can change validation-based model selection and reveal earlier stopping points in biological sequence prediction.

record.problems: The authors say the RNA similarity threshold might be insufficient and some data leakage may have occurred. Holdout test sets were not evaluated in the k-fold scheme, potentially causing short performance differences due to unequal set difficulty. The threshold precision was outside the study's scope. Many numerical results appear only in figures, and their values are not transcribed in the supplied text.
record.rows_left_out: No separately stated numerical Figure 4 or Supplementary Figure S7 values could be recovered from the supplied text; rows preserve only the described comparisons. Hyperparameter configurations and cross-validation scores are cited only as Supplementary Table S1 and are used to select settings, so omitted.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and held-out natural-label versus random-label performance under the same architecture and recipe.
Test error as width increases beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer performance under specified tuning regimes.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and compensating recipe changes.
Dropout interventions, training-set-size dependence, and interactions with augmentation and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its ranking of generalization gaps relative to other measures.
Removing examples selected by label memorization versus removing equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: All row states are cannot_determine relative to V1–V8 because their measures address a different question; this does not negate the reported partitioning effects. Background citations about random-label fitting and memorization do not constitute tests.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label fitting or comparison of natural-label and random-label test accuracy.
No comparison of convolutional and fully connected architectures.
